question.stem: A retailer runs a support assistant that summarizes text conversations for agents. Routine quality checks show that summaries often omit the resolution, so your team is considering replacement models from Model Garden. The evaluation project belongs to your company's Google Cloud organization. The shortlisted models offer playgrounds and Spaces, and already have test endpoints. You want to compare their summaries on representative conversations while minimizing additional model-serving costs. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Test each shortlisted model in its Model Garden demo playground using the same representative conversations. Compare the generated summaries for resolution coverage and select the best-performing candidate.
question.correct_explanation: The decision requires comparing actual summaries while minimizing additional model-serving costs in an organization-owned project. Model Garden demo playgrounds accept text prompts and return text responses, which fits conversation summarization. They use predeployed endpoints and incur no charges. Comparing resolution coverage provides task-specific evidence for selecting a replacement. New dedicated endpoints incur compute charges, model cards and security scans do not provide the requested summary comparison, and Model Garden Spaces is unavailable for organization-owned projects.
question.distractor_1: Deploy each shortlisted model to a new dedicated test endpoint using Model Garden. Submit the same representative conversations, compare summaries for resolution coverage, and select the best-performing candidate.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the cost goal. Model Garden self-deployment charges for the compute resources used to deploy models to endpoints. The available demo playgrounds provide the requested text comparison using predeployed endpoints at no charge.
question.distractor_2: Compare the shortlisted models using their model cards and security scan status. Select the candidate whose task description matches summarization and whose checkpoint has passed authenticity scanning.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to compare actual summaries on representative conversations. Model Garden model cards provide model information, while featured-partner checkpoint scans establish authenticity. Those checks do not generate summaries or establish whether the models capture conversation resolutions.
question.distractor_3: Launch Model Garden Spaces for each shortlisted model using its existing test endpoint. Send the same representative conversations through the sample applications, compare summaries, and select the best-performing candidate.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the project constraint. Model Garden Spaces is available only for projects that are not parented by an organization. Using an existing endpoint does not remove that restriction. Model Garden demo playgrounds provide the text-testing approach for this scenario.

verdict.reason: The key is supported: playgrounds use predeployed endpoints and incur no charges, while Spaces is only for projects not parented by an organization. Distractor 2 (model cards and scan status) can be ruled out from the stem alone, because the stem asks to compare summaries on conversations.

question.stem: A retailer runs a Gemini application that extracts color and shape attributes from catalog photos. During a cost review, the team considers model adaptation using private labeled photos already stored in Cloud Storage. The labels depend on broad visual differences rather than fine details. You want to adapt Gemini from labeled image examples while minimizing image tokens used during tuning. Company policy does not allow training photos to be publicly accessible. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Fine-tune Gemini for image understanding using labeled examples, choose lower media resolution, and reference the existing training photos through Cloud Storage URIs.
question.correct_explanation: The constraints are adaptation from labeled images, minimal image-token use, and private training photos. Gemini supervised image fine-tuning adapts the model for specialized image-understanding tasks, including product attribute extraction. Lower media resolution uses fewer tokens, matching a task that does not depend on fine detail. Cloud Storage URIs let you reference the existing photos rather than publish them. Higher resolution increases token use, prompt-design experiments do not perform supervised fine-tuning, and the HTTPS dataset-source option requires publicly available images.
question.distractor_1: Fine-tune Gemini for image understanding using labeled examples, choose higher media resolution, and reference the existing training photos through Cloud Storage URIs.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize image tokens during tuning. Higher media resolution uses more tokens to capture more detail. The catalog labels depend on broad differences, so the additional detail does not justify choosing the higher-token approach.
question.distractor_2: Use Model Garden prompt design to test catalog prompts and adjust model parameters, keeping the existing labeled training photos privately stored in Cloud Storage.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to adapt Gemini from labeled image examples. Model Garden prompt design tests prompts and adjusts model parameters; it does not run supervised image fine-tuning. Gemini image fine-tuning is the feature that adapts the model from image training examples.
question.distractor_3: Fine-tune Gemini for image understanding using labeled examples, choose lower media resolution, and reference the existing training photos through HTTPS dataset URLs.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the policy against publicly accessible training photos. Gemini image tuning accepts publicly available HTTP or HTTPS URLs as an alternative to Cloud Storage URIs. Choosing HTTPS dataset URLs therefore requires public availability; referencing the existing Cloud Storage photos avoids that requirement.

verdict.reason: Key is supported by the image-tuning doc. But D1 (higher resolution) is eliminated by the stem's "minimizing image tokens", and D2 (prompt design) by "adapt from labeled examples". The options also differ only by resolution or URL-source settings, which is config trivia.

question.stem: A freight company uses a Llama model from Model Garden to extract shipment details from customer messages. Production reviews show recurring extraction errors after several rounds of advanced prompt optimization. The model supports both parameter-efficient and full fine-tuning. Reviewers have prepared 600 high-quality labeled examples covering routine messages and the relatively rare failure cases. You want to improve extraction accuracy while minimizing tuning cost. You also want the tuning dataset to reflect the mix of messages the service receives in production. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Run managed supervised fine-tuning with LoRA on the complete reviewed dataset, retaining its representative mix of routine messages and failures.
question.correct_explanation: The decision turns on recurring errors after prompt optimization, tuning cost, and representative training data. Agent Platform supervised fine-tuning adapts a supported open model using labeled examples. LoRA updates only a subset of parameters and is more cost efficient than full fine-tuning. Using the complete reviewed dataset preserves the production message mix. Further prompting does not provide the task adaptation recommended for recurrent errors after advanced prompting proves insufficient. Full fine-tuning requires more computational resources, and repeatedly sampling only failures changes the training distribution away from production usage.
question.distractor_1: Continue optimizing the current model's prompt by adding reviewed examples from the complete dataset, retaining its representative mix of messages.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails to address the recurring extraction errors that remain after advanced prompt optimization. Agent Platform recommends moving from prompting to fine-tuning when prompting is insufficient and recurrent errors need correction. The company already has hundreds of high-quality labeled examples suitable for that adaptation.
question.distractor_2: Run managed supervised fine-tuning with full fine-tuning on the complete reviewed dataset, retaining its representative mix of routine messages and failures.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize tuning cost. Full fine-tuning updates all model parameters and demands more computational resources. Agent Platform supports LoRA for this model, which updates a subset of parameters and is more cost efficient.
question.distractor_3: Run managed supervised fine-tuning with LoRA on a dataset built by repeatedly sampling the reviewed failure cases to emphasize difficult messages.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement for training data to reflect the production message mix. Repeatedly sampling only the relatively rare failures excludes routine messages and changes that mix. Agent Platform tuning guidance calls for training data that reflects the prompt distribution, format, and context encountered in production.

verdict.reason: LoRA is documented as more cost efficient than full fine-tuning. But the stem's production-mix want eliminates distractor 3, and its note that prompt optimization already failed eliminates distractor 1. Only distractor 2 needs product knowledge.

question.stem: Extract text and paragraph boundaries from scanned customer letters for a new compliance review application. Your Document AI processors will run in one project, while the input documents are held in a Cloud Storage bucket in another project in the same organization. The processors will read the documents directly from that bucket. Company policy does not allow document storage or processing outside the European Union. You want to give the processing workflow access to the input bucket while minimizing the permissions granted. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Create Document AI Document OCR processors in the European Union and use the matching regional endpoint. Grant Storage Object Viewer on the input bucket to the Document AI service agent of the processor project.
question.correct_explanation: The application needs OCR output, European Union storage and processing, and minimal permissions for cross-project input access. Document AI Document OCR processors return full text and paragraph information. Choosing the European Union processor location and matching regional endpoint addresses the location policy. Granting Storage Object Viewer on the input bucket to the processor project's Document AI service agent provides the required cross-project read access. The alternatives use the wrong location, grant access to the wrong principal, or grant an administrative role instead of the required read access.
question.distractor_1: Create Document AI Document OCR processors in the United States and use the matching regional endpoint. Grant Storage Object Viewer on the input bucket to the Document AI service agent of the processor project.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This violates the European Union storage and processing policy. Document AI stores and processes processor data in the selected location. Processors created in the United States therefore fail that policy even when cross-project permissions are correct.
question.distractor_2: Create Document AI Document OCR processors in the European Union and use the matching regional endpoint. Grant Storage Object Viewer on the input bucket to the application's service account that submits requests to the processors.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement for processors to read the cross-project input bucket directly. Document AI requires Storage Object Viewer on that bucket for the Document AI service agent of the processor project. Granting the role to the requesting application's service account does not grant access to that service agent.
question.distractor_3: Create Document AI Document OCR processors in the European Union and use the matching regional endpoint. Grant Storage Admin on the input bucket to the Document AI service agent of the processor project.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This violates the requirement to minimize granted permissions. Document AI cross-project input access requires Storage Object Viewer for the service agent. Granting Storage Admin uses an administrative role where read access is sufficient, contrary to the principle of granting only the permissions needed.

verdict.reason: Distractors 1 and 3 can be eliminated from the stem alone: the EU-only policy rules out the US option, and the minimal-permissions want rules out Storage Admin. The docs also never say Document OCR returns text and paragraphs, though the explanation claims it.

question.stem: Prototype alternative ticket-response models for a customer-support service that already uses an open model. Your team is migrating its experiments to Google Cloud, where researchers will continue editing and rerunning training cells interactively in notebooks. The migration uses an existing organization-owned project. You want to fine-tune several supported foundation models from Model Garden with your ticket-response examples while minimizing notebook setup work. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Open the candidates' tuning notebooks from their Model Garden cards, then adapt and run the training cells in Agent Platform Workbench with your ticket-response examples.
question.correct_explanation: The migration retains interactive notebook experiments in an organization-owned project and requires fine-tuning several models with minimal notebook setup. Supported Model Garden cards provide tuning notebooks, giving researchers a starting point for each candidate. Agent Platform Workbench provides JupyterLab and preinstalled deep learning packages for editing and running those notebooks. Inference parameter experiments do not perform the requested fine-tuning, console-based pipeline runs do not retain interactive training cells, and Model Garden Spaces is unavailable in organization-owned projects.
question.distractor_1: Open the candidates' inference notebooks from Model Garden in Agent Platform Workbench, then experiment with prompts, temperature, and output length using your ticket-response examples.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the fine-tuning requirement. Model Garden exposes temperature and output length as parameters for testing model responses, and its inference examples use those parameters when requesting predictions. Experimenting with those controls does not execute the tuning workflow needed to train on your ticket-response examples.
question.distractor_2: Use Model Garden fine-tuning pipelines for candidates that offer them, supply your ticket-response examples, and iterate by launching tuning runs through Agent Platform Pipelines.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the retained interactive notebook workflow. Model Garden's fine-tuning pipeline action opens Agent Platform Pipelines, where tuning starts by creating a run. This option iterates through pipeline submissions rather than editing and rerunning notebook training cells. Model Garden's tuning notebooks provide the required notebook approach.
question.distractor_3: Launch Model Garden Spaces for the supported candidates in the migration project, then open their tuning notebooks in Agent Platform Workbench to run your adaptation experiments.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the project constraint. Model Garden Spaces is available only for projects that are not parented by an organization, so it cannot be launched in the existing organization-owned project. Opening the candidates' tuning notebooks directly avoids that unavailable prerequisite.

verdict.reason: Docs support tuning notebooks, pipelines, and the Spaces org restriction. But the key explanation's Workbench claims (JupyterLab, preinstalled packages) are not in the supplied text, and the cited notebook URI opens Colab. Distractor 1 is eliminable from the fine-tuning wording alone.

question.stem: A consumer lender uses a running BigQuery ML boosted-tree model to identify loans likely to miss a payment. Its daily explanation job uses exact feature attributions and now finishes too late for loan officers. Approximate contributions are acceptable to both loan officers and auditors. You want to minimize explanation runtime while retaining feature contributions for individual loan predictions. Auditors want an overall summary showing the average magnitude of each feature's prediction contributions across the evaluation loans. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Keep the boosted-tree model. Use approximate feature contribution with ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT for individual loans and ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN for the audit summary.
question.correct_explanation: The lender needs faster explanations, individual prediction contributions, and an audit summary of average contribution magnitudes. BigQuery ML supports approximate feature contribution for boosted trees, which is faster and simpler than Tree SHAP. ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT provides local feature attributions for individual predictions. ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN returns the mean absolute attribution for each feature across the evaluation dataset, matching the audit requirement. Tree SHAP fails the runtime goal, global explanations alone fail the individual explanation requirement, and training-based feature importance fails the requested audit calculation.
question.distractor_1: Keep the boosted-tree model. Use exact Tree SHAP attribution with ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT for individual loans and ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN for the audit summary.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize explanation runtime when approximate contributions are acceptable. BigQuery ML describes approximate feature contribution as faster and simpler than Tree SHAP. Continuing to compute exact Tree SHAP values retains the slower explanation method.
question.distractor_2: Keep the boosted-tree model. Use approximate feature contribution with ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN for both individual loan explanations and the overall audit summary.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement for feature contributions for individual loan predictions. ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN aggregates attributions into mean absolute values across the evaluation dataset. Those global values do not provide each loan's local feature attributions; ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT provides those explanations.
question.distractor_3: Keep the boosted-tree model. Use approximate feature contribution with ML.EXPLAIN_PREDICT for individual loans and ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE for the audit summary.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the audit requirement to summarize average prediction contribution magnitudes across evaluation loans. ML.FEATURE_IMPORTANCE returns Gini index-based importance describing each feature's usefulness during tree model construction. ML.GLOBAL_EXPLAIN instead returns mean absolute prediction attributions across the evaluation dataset.

verdict.reason: The key is supported by the docs: approximate feature contribution is faster than Tree SHAP, EXPLAIN_PREDICT is local, and GLOBAL_EXPLAIN is the mean absolute attribution. The style check fails because the stem stacks three wants: runtime, individual contributions, and the auditor summary.

question.stem: A retailer's shopping assistant returns product suggestions in near real time through an Agent Platform online endpoint. Monitoring shows that incoming requests bypass the model's input normalization and outgoing responses expose internal model fields rather than the assistant's customer-facing suggestion format. You want to correct these inference transformations while minimizing the serving infrastructure code your team maintains. Which approach should you use?
question.correct_answer: Implement input normalization and response formatting in a custom Predictor using custom inference routines. Build the container with Agent Platform SDK for Python, test it locally, and deploy it to an online endpoint.
question.correct_explanation: The assistant needs near-real-time suggestions, corrected input and output transformations, and minimal serving infrastructure code. Custom inference routines support normalization through preprocessing and response formatting through postprocessing. Agent Platform SDK for Python builds the container and supports local testing, while providing the HTTP model server. Deployment to an online endpoint preserves near-real-time serving. Batch inference fails the interactive timing requirement, Model Armor safety screening does not implement the required transformations, and a handwritten server adds infrastructure code.
question.distractor_1: Implement input normalization and response formatting in a custom Predictor using custom inference routines. Build the container with Agent Platform SDK for Python, then run batch inference periodically and deliver the resulting suggestions.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the near-real-time suggestion requirement. Batch inference scores groups of data at a regular cadence, whereas online inference provides near-real-time scoring for live applications. Correct preprocessing and postprocessing do not make periodic batch results suitable for this interactive workload.
question.distractor_2: Place Model Armor around the existing online inference service. Use its incoming prompt screening as the preprocessing stage and its outgoing response screening as the postprocessing stage, then return the screened suggestions.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to correct input normalization and customer-facing response formatting. Model Armor screens prompts and responses for safety issues and can redact sensitive information. These safety checks do not implement the model's normalization or the assistant's business-specific response format. Custom inference routines provide those transformation capabilities.
question.distractor_3: Implement input normalization and response formatting in a handwritten HTTP model server. Write its Dockerfile, build the custom serving container, test it locally, and deploy it to an Agent Platform online endpoint.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize maintained serving infrastructure code. The approach adds a handwritten HTTP model server and Dockerfile. Custom inference routines provide the model server and container-building workflow while allowing the same preprocessing, postprocessing, local testing, and online deployment.

verdict.reason: The key is supported by the custom inference routines doc (pre/postprocessing, server and Dockerfile provided, local testing). Distractor 1 (batch) is eliminated by the stem's own 'near real time online endpoint' wording, and distractor 3 is largely eliminated by 'minimizing code', so not all distractors need domain knowledge.

question.stem: A retailer recently deployed a Gemini assistant that drafts customer-service replies, but reviewers keep correcting its tone. Your SQL team stores 1,000 customer prompts and approved replies in BigQuery, with a reviewer-maintained marker identifying 200 evaluation examples. You want to fine-tune Gemini on these examples while minimizing data preparation. Company policy reserves the marked examples for evaluation and the remaining examples for training. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Create a tuned BigQuery ML remote model from the prompt and approved-response columns using SQL. Use a custom split based on the reviewer designation, then evaluate the tuned model with EVALUATE.
question.correct_explanation: The solution needs to fine-tune Gemini, minimize data preparation, and preserve the reviewer-designated split. BigQuery ML performs supervised tuning using prompt and label columns supplied through AS SELECT, so the existing table can supply the examples directly. A custom split uses a Boolean column to assign evaluation and training rows according to the reviewer designation. EVALUATE checks whether tuning improved the model for this use case; improvement is not guaranteed. Prompting does not perform supervised tuning, the SDK approach requires preparing dataset files, and a random split does not preserve the designated evaluation examples.
question.distractor_1: Create a BigQuery ML remote model referencing a supported Gemini model. Include approved replies as examples in AI.GENERATE_TEXT prompts, then have reviewers assess generated replies using the reserved evaluation examples.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to fine-tune Gemini. Including examples in inference prompts is prompt design. BigQuery ML supervised tuning requires supplying training examples through AS SELECT; creating a remote model and generating text with example-filled prompts does not perform that training.
question.distractor_2: Export the prompt and approved-response pairs into training and validation files in Cloud Storage according to the reviewer designation. Fine-tune Gemini through the Google Gen AI SDK, then evaluate the tuned model.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize data preparation. The Google Gen AI SDK tuning approach uses dataset files in Cloud Storage, adding export and file preparation work. BigQuery ML can select the existing prompt and label columns directly from the BigQuery table while preserving the designated split.
question.distractor_3: Create a tuned BigQuery ML remote model from the prompt and approved-response columns using SQL. Randomly reserve 20% of examples for evaluation, then evaluate the tuned model with EVALUATE.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the policy requiring the reviewer-designated examples to remain in their assigned sets. BigQuery ML random splitting assigns rows randomly, so matching the evaluation percentage does not preserve the designated rows. A custom split uses the reviewer-maintained Boolean marker to assign each row to training or evaluation.

verdict.reason: The key matches the docs (AS SELECT tuning, CUSTOM split on a BOOL column, EVALUATE). But distractors 1 and 3 can be ruled out from the stem alone: prompting isn't fine-tuning, and a random 20% split contradicts the stated policy to reserve the marked examples.

question.stem: A publisher runs an article-summary service that helps editors review incoming stories. Monitoring shows that summaries increasingly omit key facts. The application's Google Cloud project belongs to the company organization, and you have shortlisted replacement models in Model Garden that support demo playgrounds. You want to compare their summaries of representative articles while minimizing setup work. Company policy does not allow model evaluation outside the application's existing project. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Open each shortlisted model's card and use its demo playground to submit representative articles. Compare the summaries and select the model that best meets the task's needs.
question.correct_explanation: The selection requires comparing actual summaries, minimizing setup, and keeping evaluation in the existing project. Model Garden demo playgrounds accept text prompts and return text responses through predeployed endpoints, enabling direct comparison with little setup. Model Garden Spaces cannot launch in organization-parented projects. Deploying endpoints and building an app adds setup work, while deployment specifications do not demonstrate summarization quality.
question.distractor_1: Open each shortlisted model's card and launch Model Garden Spaces in the existing project. Submit representative articles through the sample apps and select the model producing the best summaries.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the requirement to evaluate in the existing project. Model Garden Spaces is available only for projects that are not parented by an organization, so it cannot launch in this application's project.
question.distractor_2: Deploy each shortlisted model to a new endpoint in the existing project and build a comparison app. Submit representative articles and select the model producing the best summaries.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize setup work. It introduces model deployment and application development, whereas Model Garden demo playgrounds already provide predeployed endpoints and a prompt interface for testing text responses.
question.distractor_3: Review each shortlisted model's deployment specifications and compare its verified hardware and serving container. Select the model with the configuration that appears best suited to the article-summary service.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to compare summaries of representative articles. Model Garden deployment specifications identify verified machine types, accelerators, and container images. Reviewing those specifications does not produce summaries to assess; demo playgrounds let you submit the articles and inspect model responses.

verdict.reason: Distractor 3 (review deployment specs) is eliminated by the stem alone, since the stem asks to compare summaries. Distractor 2 is largely eliminated by "minimizing setup." Docs don't say playgrounds run inside the project, but the key's explanation claims it. The policy line is ambiguous.

question.stem: You work for a retailer whose catalog service uses Gemini to extract attributes from product photos. The team is updating the model using reviewed photo-and-attribute examples, but image-token usage in tuning runs has grown. Trials show that moderate image detail preserves small label text as accurately as full detail, which adds extra image crops. The lowest-detail representation misses that text. You want to adapt the base model to the retailer's attribute conventions while minimizing image tokens used for tuning. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Use supervised image fine-tuning for Gemini with the reviewed photo-and-attribute examples. Choose the least detailed image representation that preserved label text in trials.
question.correct_explanation: The model needs adaptation from labeled images, accurate extraction of label text, and reduced image-token usage during tuning. Gemini supervised image fine-tuning supports adapting base models for product attribute extraction. The trials establish that moderate detail preserves the necessary text, so retaining additional detail is unnecessary. Lower detail fails label accuracy, the default high-detail representation adds tokens for extra image crops, and Model Garden prompt testing does not perform model fine-tuning.
question.distractor_1: Use supervised image fine-tuning for Gemini with the reviewed photo-and-attribute examples. Choose the lowest-detail image representation available to reduce image-token usage throughout training.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the label-text accuracy requirement. Gemini image resolution controls how much detail the model perceives as well as image-token usage. The trials established that the lowest-detail representation misses required text, so its token savings sacrifice necessary information.
question.distractor_2: Use supervised image fine-tuning for Gemini with the reviewed photo-and-attribute examples. Retain the default image representation throughout training to preserve detailed visual information.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to minimize image tokens during tuning. Gemini image tuning defaults to high resolution, which adds tokens for additional image crops. Full detail produces those crops in this workload, while moderate detail already preserves label accuracy.
question.distractor_3: Test revised instructions against the reviewed examples in Model Garden prompt design. Select the best prompt and keep the existing Gemini model for catalog extraction.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the requirement to adapt the base model through tuning. Model Garden prompt design sends test prompts and optionally configures model parameters. Gemini supervised image fine-tuning is the approach that adapts the base model from the reviewed image examples.

verdict.reason: The stem states that lowest detail misses label text and that full detail adds extra crops. That eliminates distractors 1 and 2 without product knowledge. Options 1–3 differ only by media-resolution setting, which is config-level. Key and docs are accurate.

question.stem: Your distribution company runs a scikit-learn invoice anomaly classifier to help reviewers identify suspicious supplier invoices. The billing system sends comma-separated invoice records to an Agent Platform endpoint. The classifier returns a review decision and internal supplier metadata, which a recent security incident exposed in the reviewer console. You want the serving layer to return only the review decision while minimizing custom server maintenance. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Build custom inference routines with a custom Handler to deserialize invoice records and a custom Predictor to postprocess the review decision. Deploy the generated container to the Agent Platform endpoint.
question.correct_explanation: The existing interface requires deserializing comma-separated records, the response must contain only the review decision, and custom server maintenance should be minimized. A custom Handler handles non-JSON request deserialization. A custom Predictor implements postprocessing that selects the review decision from the model output. Custom inference routines provide the HTTP server and container-building workflow. The default Handler does not provide the required custom deserialization, inheriting SklearnPredictor's prediction behavior does not add the required output filtering, and writing an HTTP server adds avoidable maintenance.
question.distractor_1: Build custom inference routines with the default Handler and a custom Predictor to postprocess the review decision. Deploy the generated container to the existing Agent Platform endpoint.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails compatibility with the billing system's comma-separated requests. Custom inference routines use a custom Handler for deserializing non-JSON inference requests. Customizing the Predictor's output processing does not supply that request-handling customization.
question.distractor_2: Build custom inference routines with a custom Handler to deserialize invoice records and the distributed SklearnPredictor for model execution. Deploy the generated container to the Agent Platform endpoint.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the requirement to return only the review decision. The custom Handler supplies request deserialization, while SklearnPredictor supplies model loading and prediction behavior. The approach does not implement custom postprocessing to remove supplier metadata from the classifier's output.
question.distractor_3: Build a custom serving container with your own HTTP server to deserialize invoice records and filter responses to the review decision. Deploy that container to the Agent Platform endpoint.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the goal of minimizing custom server maintenance. It makes the team responsible for its HTTP server and container construction. Custom inference routines support the same request deserialization and response postprocessing while providing the model server and container-building workflow.

verdict.reason: The key matches the docs: a custom Handler for CSV input and a custom Predictor for postprocessing. But the stem's 'minimizing custom server maintenance' rules out distractor 3 without product knowledge. The key is also marginally the longest option, which breaks O4.

question.stem: You are building an online product-recommendation service for a retailer's launch event on Agent Platform. Load tests of your TPU-optimized custom container on the chosen Cloud TPU machine type show that each replica sustains 100 requests per second. Launch traffic is forecast at 400 requests per second. The container's HTTP server reports healthy before model loading finishes. You want to handle forecast traffic while minimizing serving cost. You also want new replicas to receive requests only after their models are ready. What should you do?
question.correct_answer: Deploy on Cloud TPU with four minimum replicas, and configure a custom health probe that succeeds only after model loading completes. Size serving capacity using the per-replica load test.
question.correct_explanation: The throughput forecast requires four replicas at the tested capacity. Cloud TPU deployments on Agent Platform always use the minimum replica count and ignore the maximum, so four minimum replicas provide the required capacity. Cloud TPU machines are billed hourly, making additional replicas unnecessary expense for this forecast. A custom health probe that succeeds only after loading prevents premature traffic routing. One minimum replica cannot autoscale to four on Cloud TPU, eight minimum replicas increase cost, and default health checks would accept the server's premature healthy response.
question.distractor_1: Deploy on Cloud TPU with one minimum replica and four maximum replicas, and configure a custom health probe that succeeds only after model loading completes. Rely on autoscaling for launch traffic.
question.distractor_1_explanation: This fails the forecast throughput requirement. Agent Platform does not support autoscaling for Cloud TPU deployments: it always uses the minimum replica count and ignores the maximum. The deployment therefore uses one replica, whose tested capacity is only 100 requests per second.
question.distractor_2: Deploy on Cloud TPU with eight minimum replicas, and configure a custom health probe that succeeds only after model loading completes. Keep all eight replicas provisioned for launch traffic.
question.distractor_2_explanation: This fails the cost-minimization requirement. Four replicas cover the forecast at the tested per-replica capacity. Agent Platform uses the configured minimum count for Cloud TPU deployments, and Cloud TPU machines are billed hourly, so provisioning eight replicas incurs unnecessary serving expense.
question.distractor_3: Deploy on Cloud TPU with four minimum replicas, and retain default HTTP health checks against the existing server. Use those successful responses to admit new replicas into the serving pool.
question.distractor_3_explanation: This fails the readiness requirement. Agent Platform's default HTTP health checks treat a successful response as healthy even if model loading is incomplete. Because this server reports healthy prematurely, traffic can arrive before the model is ready. A custom health probe should succeed only after loading completes.

verdict.reason: Key is supported (TPU ignores maxReplicaCount; custom health probe fixes premature 200 OK). But distractor 3 (default HTTP checks) is contradicted by the stem, which says the server reports healthy early and replicas must wait for readiness. Distractor 2 is also eliminable by arithmetic and the cost want.
